voiceover.text: So, why screen people before they exercise? Exercise lowers the risk of almost every major chronic disease. So why would a fitness professional make someone answer health questions before letting them start? Write down two reasons. Then add one thing you think a short questionnaire couldn't possibly pick up.

scenes.title: benefit is spread, risk is concentrated

voiceover.text: The puzzle goes away once you separate two kinds of risk. Across a whole population, regular activity lowers the risk of most chronic diseases. But for one person during a hard session, the heart rate, blood pressure and the heart's workload rise sharply, as you saw in Year 11. That briefly raises the risk of a serious event, and the extra risk sits almost entirely in people with heart disease they don't know about. Pre-exercise screening is a structured check to find that small group before they're asked to work hard. It does three jobs. Safety: spot conditions that make hard or unsupervised exercise unsafe right now. Duty of care: the legal and ethical duty to take reasonable steps to prevent harm you could foresee. And personalisation: the same answers describe the person's history, medicines, injuries and goals. So screening isn't there because exercise is dangerous.

scenes.title: the questionnaire: Stage 1 and question seven

voiceover.text: In Australia the standard tool is the APSS, the Adult Pre-Exercise Screening System. It has two stages. Stage 1 is compulsory for everyone. Questions one to six ask about known heart disease or stroke, unexplained chest pain, feeling faint or dizzy during activity, a recent asthma attack needing urgent care, trouble controlling diabetes, and any other condition needing special care. If all six are no, question seven asks how active you are, as weighted minutes: light and moderate minutes, plus twice the vigorous minutes, because a vigorous minute is about twice the work. Say a nineteen-year-old walks ninety minutes a week and plays thirty minutes of hard football. That's ninety plus sixty, a hundred and fifty. Below one fifty, the advice is light to moderate activity, built up gradually. At one fifty or more, continue at your current level.

Stage 2 is recommended, done with an exercise professional, and reviews risk factors such as age, family history, smoking and blood pressure, to shape the program. Notice it doesn't sort people into fixed risk categories.

scenes.title: acting on the answers: guidance, scope and judgement

voiceover.text: A screen only matters if someone acts on it. A yes to any of questions one to six means the person should get guidance from a doctor or an appropriate allied health professional before exercising. That isn't a diagnosis. It's about scope of practice, the limits of what a professional is trained and allowed to do. A personal trainer can't diagnose chest pain, so they make a referral, directing the person to someone who can. Stage 2 works differently. There's no automatic referral. The professional uses judgement. With significant or several risk factors, they may seek further medical advice. Otherwise they use what they've learned to set a safer starting intensity, a slower progression, or closer supervision.

Be precise about the limits too. A questionnaire is a filter, not a diagnosis. First, it relies on self-report. People may not know they have a condition, may forget, or may play down symptoms because they want to train. Second, it can't see disease with no symptoms, and that's exactly the group screening most wants to find. Third, it's a snapshot. Health changes, so people should be screened again at intervals, and after any injury, illness or pregnancy. So it's the first step, followed by watching during sessions and teaching people the warning signs.

scenes.title: from screen to a personalised program

voiceover.text: And that's where personalisation starts. Back to our nineteen-year-old. All six answers are no. Question seven gives exactly a hundred and fifty weighted minutes, so it counts, and the advice is to continue at that level. In the Stage 2 review, they mention a fully healed ankle sprain from two years ago, and they want to start running. So the professional sets a starting load from where they actually are, builds running volume gradually, and adds ankle strength and balance work early. It's the first information you have about one person, and the start of their program.
Two things to remember. Benefit is spread, but acute risk is concentrated. And a questionnaire is a filter, not a diagnosis.

Two exam questions. First. Person one, aged thirty-eight, has type 2 diabetes, with blood sugar unstable for several weeks, and hasn't seen a doctor. Person two, aged forty-four, answers no to questions one to six, smokes, does under a hundred and fifty weighted minutes a week, and their father had a heart attack at fifty-two. For each, follow the APSS. Pause here to answer.

Person one answers yes to the diabetes control question, so they should get guidance from a doctor before starting. Person two passes Stage 1, and question seven means light to moderate activity, built up gradually. In Stage 2, smoking and family history call for judgement, maybe further medical advice, and a cautious start. The classic mistake is giving person two a fixed risk category.

Second. A sixty-year-old answers no to questions one to six and does under a hundred and fifty weighted minutes a week. In Stage 2, they report a fully recovered knee replacement from four years ago, blood pressure medication, and a goal of walking ten kilometres in six months. Explain what the APSS recommends, and how Stage 2 should shape their first four weeks. Pause here to answer.

Under one fifty means light to moderate walking, built up gradually. The knee means low-impact, steady progression in distance, with strength work around the knee. Blood pressure medicine means moderate intensity, monitoring, and judgement about checking with their doctor. So weeks one to four might be three walks a week, adding about ten minutes each week. The classic mistake is starting at the ten-kilometre goal.

So screen everyone, act on any Stage 1 yes, use Stage 2 with judgement, and treat the result as the start of a program. Once someone's on the green path, the next question is where they actually are now. That means testing. What makes a fitness test worth running?
